The facetted side by side bar above illustrates comparison between each pair of twins on their genetic share from different regions. Although I had to decide on one specific test kit to show the comparison - which might cause some reliability issue - but I believed that would be the most precise way to show the relationship between each twin (A/B) without some confounding variables. Looking at tiny differences between each A/B twins, we can see the slight genetic differences.

The graphic above tells the story of uncertainty in consumer DNA testing. While we might assume that reading DNA is an exact science, this visualization reveals that different kits interpret the exact same material (twins) differently. By plotting the estimated percentage on the X-axis and grouping by ancestry region on the Y-axis, we can clearly see the “spread” of the colored dots. It proves that these kits are giving us estimates based on their specific reference panels, not absolute facts.

Exercise 2

Challenge: Identify issues with this graphic and make something better.

Issues

  1. The y-axis runs from 0.00 to 1.25, but the data labels show totals of “478,123” and “496,234”. The y-axis is likely meant to represent units of 100,000 (so 0.50 means 50,000 touchpoints per month), but missing the “in 100,000s” label forces the audience to do mental math to figure out what the bars represent.

  2. Stacked bars are great for showing totals, but terrible for showing individual trends. Because the “Phone” segment at the bottom fluctuates, the baselines for “Chat” and “Email” are constantly moving up and down. This makes it visually impossible to tell if chat or email volumes are actually trending up or down over time.

  3. The horizontal brackets showing the yearly totals (478,123 and 496,234) have black dots that float arbitrarily and cut right through the data bars, creating visual clutter.

Possible Improvements

  1. label the y-axis with (in 100K) to show that 0.5 represents 50,000.

  2. Use a Line Chart with three distinct lines—one for Phone, one for Chat, and one for Email. This will show individual trend of each channel type to resolve the problem of stacked bar.

  3. Exclude the totals (478,123 and 496,234) from the new generated line graph, however, if the information is critical or necessary, it is always possible to add in the description paragraph afterwards.

a Searching through dataset website I found

Referred Dataset-new CSV

I was always curious about what type of people, or what factors of environment causes the students to push their study hours more. From the Graphics above, there are four factors I chose from a big dataset to show their relationships to daily hours of study. To be honest, most of them were out of my expectation. Academic pressure score (scatterplot) and Burnout level (green bar) didn’t show much effect on the study hours; however we could argue that middle range of both variables (Medium burnout level or 5-6 academic pressure score) could cause higher study hours. The stress level of study and the average study hour correlated positively. The most interesting thing was that the average study hour of students decreased significantly as they turned upperclassmen (junior and senior). This might be because of the internships, or job searchings, however, I think it is caused by their tiredness from school and academics that they pursued since freshmen year.

b

about the data source The data used for this graphic is a dataset containing 7,500 records of user smartphone habits.

dataset: Where I downloaded - Raw Dataset (csv)

Maximizing the Data-Ink Ratio (Decluttering): In accordance with Tufte’s principles, non-essential visual clutter was stripped away. I removed the default background gridlines to give the data room to breathe. I also removed redundant legends from the Stress and Age charts, as the X-axis labels already provided that information clearly.

Preattentive Attributes (Color): In the primary scatterplot, color is used as a preattentive attribute to immediately separate users by their “Addicted Status.” By using the high-contrast color scheme (red vs blue), the viewer instantly processes the “wall” where daily screen time crosses into addiction without having to actively read the axes.

Data Integrity (Honest Scales): A common pitfall in interactive dashboards is allowing axes to auto-zoom when data is filtered, which can mislead the viewer about the size of a subset. To maintain visual integrity, I hardcoded the Y-axis scales. When a viewer highlights a small cluster of users, the bars shrink relative to the maximum population, maintaining an honest representation of the total dataset. Although this might cause difficulties for the viewrs to read the data at small cluster, I believed it would be a better choice compare to when the axes scales shift every single time.

Layering for Context: Instead of just showing a sleep distribution histogram, I layered a calculated average rule line (the red vertical line) with exact text over the bars. This allows the viewer to see both the shape of the data and the summary statistic simultaneously. Also, this would help the viewers to know the changes in average even in small clusters where the bars are very low due to fixed y-axis scale.

Alternatives In an earlier iteration, the bottom-right chart simply showed a single bar for “Average Sleep Hours.” I removed this and showed graphic of a full Histogram Distribution. An average value completely hides the spread of the data. By showing the distribution, we can uncover a much more interesting narrative: highly addicted users don’t all get 6 hours of sleep; rather, they are bimodal—some get 4 hours, while others crash and get 9.

Exercise 5

  1. An encoding channel other than x or y

Where I used it: the color channel extensively.

How it was used: In the scatterplot, I mapped color to the addicted_label to clearly separate the addicted users (blue) from the non-addicted users (red). It was also used in the Age chart (using the teals color scheme) and the Stress chart to give each category a distinct visual identity.

  1. Layers

Where I used it: The “Sleep Distribution & Average” chart in the bottom right.

How it was used: I used the “layer” to stack three completely different marks on top of the same X/Y axis. I layered a bar mark (the orange histogram), a rule mark (the red vertical line), and a text mark (the exact numerical average) all in one chart space to deliver precise informations.

  1. Facets

*Note: Although the graphic looks like I used facet to sort multiple graphs and plots, faceting is used to split a single chart type into multiple small multiples based on a category. Because I wanted to show completely different types of charts together, I used concatenation instead.

  1. Concatenation or Repeat

Where I used it: The entire layout of the dashboard.

How it was used: I used “vconcat” (vertical concatenation) to split the graphic into a top half and a bottom half. Inside those halves, I used “hconcat” (horizontal concatenation) to place the individual charts side-by-side.

  1. Non-default settings for a channel’s scale or guide

Where I used it: Across almost all the charts (Axes, Domains, and Colors).

How it was used: - Scale (Domain): As mentioned in Exercise 4, I applied “scale”: {“domain”: [0, 900]} to the Y-axes of the bar charts. This non-default setting locks the axis in place so the bars dynamically shrink when you filter the data, rather than the chart zooming in confusingly.

  • Scale (Color): I overrode the default color palettes by specifying “scale”: {“scheme”: “set1”} and “scheme”: “teals”.

  • Guide (Axis): I used “axis”: {“labelAngle”: 0} to force the text labels to sit horizontal instead of tilting diagonally.

  1. Tooltips

Where I used it: The scatterplot dots.

How it was used: I fed an array of fields (line 55 - line 59) into the “tooltip” channel. Now, hovering over a single, anonymous dot reveals a pop-up with 5 specific data points (Age, Gender, Screen Time, Sleep Hours, Addicted Status).

  1. Another kind of interaction (Brushing)

Where I used it: The main “Screen Time vs. Work/Study Time” scatterplot.

How it was used: I defined a parameter called “brush” configured for “interval”. This allows the user to click and drag a rectangular box over a cluster of dots. We then applied a “transform”: [{“filter”: {“param”: “brush”}}] to the other three charts, turning the brush into an interactive, cross-filtering tool that updates the whole dashboard in real-time.

Exercise 6

a. Advanced Vega-Lite Features

  1. Global Theming through the config Block (Exercise 3 & 4): Rather than manually styling the axes, borders, and fonts for every single chart individually, I utilized the top-level "config" block at the end of my JSON specifications. For example, in the complex dashboard for Exercise 4, I used "config": {"view": {"stroke": "transparent"}, "concat": {"spacing": 40}, "axis": {"grid": false}}.

  2. Small Multiples through the row Encoding Channel (Exercise 1): To show how different testing kits estimated ancestry for the same individuals, I needed to split the scatterplot. Instead of building a complex, nested "facet" block, I used the "row" encoding channel. This is a highly efficient, advanced shortcut in Vega-Lite that instantly generates vertically stacked small multiples, giving each twin their own dedicated horizontal track.

  3. Calculated Expressions in Headers (Exercise 1): In the faceting for the twin genetic share graphic, I didn’t want the panel headers to just show bare numbers or raw data strings. Inside the "header" block of the facet encoding, I used "labelExpr": "\'Pair \' + datum.value". This feature allows you to write expressions to dynamically concatenate text and data, resulting in much cleaner, reader-friendly labels like “Pair 1” instead of just “1”.

b. Application of Graphic Design Principles

  1. Titles as Storytelling Tools (Wilke): Claus O. Wilke emphasizes that text is a crucial graphical element and that titles should ideally bring the core message or provide instructions, rather than just stating the variables. In Exercise 4, instead of a generic title like “Scatterplot of Screen Time,” I used “The Extremes of Smartphone Addiction” alongside an instructional subtitle (“Highlight a cluster…”).
    • Citation: Wilke, C. O. (2019). Fundamentals of Data Visualization. O’Reilly Media. Chapter 22: “Titles, captions, and tables.” (Available at: https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/figure-titles-captions.html)
  2. Maximizing the Data-Ink Ratio (Tufte): Edward Tufte famously advocates for erasing non-data-ink to let the actual data stand out. Across my portfolio (especially Exercises 3 and 4), I aggressively stripped away default programmatic clutter. I explicitly removed the chart borders using "view": {"stroke": "transparent"} and removed the distracting background gridlines ("axis": {"grid": false}).
    • Citation: Tufte, E. R. (2001). The Visual Display of Quantitative Information (2nd ed.). Graphics Press. Chapter 4: “Data-Ink and Graphical Redesign.” pdf
  3. Avoiding Stacked Bars for Trend Comparisons (Healy): In Exercise 2, the original graphic used a stacked bar chart to show changes in customer touchpoints over time. Kieran Healy points out that stacked bar charts make it extremely difficult to compare the trends of the inner or upper segments because they lack a common baseline. Following this principle, I redesigned the graphic into a line chart with three distinct lines. This allows the viewer to easily and accurately track the independent trajectory of Phone, Chat, and Email touchpoints.
    • Citation: Healy, K. (2019). Data Visualization: A practical introduction. Princeton University Press. Chapter 1: “Look at data.” (Available at: https://socviz.co/lookatdata.html)

```{r}
    "subtitleFontSize": 15},

  "vconcat":[
    {
     "height": 200,
     "width": 200,
  
     "title": {
     "text": "Regions",
     "orient": "bottom",
     "anchor": "middle",
     "offset": 15}, 

     "mark": {"type": "bar", "tooltip": true},

     "encoding": {
        "facet": {
          "field": "pair",
          "columns": 3,
          "title": null,
          "header": {
            "labelExpr": "\'Pair \' + datum.value" 
          }
        },
        "x": {
          "field": "region",
          "type": "nominal",
          "axis": {"labelAngle":45},
          "title": null
        },
        "y":{
          "field": "Ancestry",
          "type": "quantitative",
          "title": "Genetic Share"
        },
        "xOffset": {
          "field": "id"
        },
        "color": {
          "field": "id",
          "title": "A/B"
        }
      },
      "resolve": {
        "axis":{"x": "independent"}
      }
    }
  ],
  "config": {
    "view": {"stroke": ""},
    "axis": {"grid": true, "gridOpacity": 0.5}
  }
}
'|> as_vegaspec()
```

The facetted side by side bar above illustrates comparison between each
pair of twins on their genetic share from different regions. Although I
had to decide on one specific test kit to show the comparison - which
might cause some reliability issue - but I believed that would be the
most precise way to show the relationship between each twin (A/B)
without some confounding variables. Looking at tiny differences between
each A/B twins, we can see the slight genetic differences.

```{r}
library(vegawidget)
'
{
  "$schema": "https://vega.github.io/schema/vega-lite/v6.json",
  "data": {
    "url": "https://calvin-data304.netlify.app/data/twins-genetics-long.json"
  },
  "title": {
    "text": "Consistency Across DNA Kits",
    "subtitle": "How different testing kits estimate ancestry for the same individuals",
    "fontSize": 18,
    "anchor": "middle"
  },
  "height": 100,
  "width": 600,
  "mark": {
    "type": "circle",
    "size": 150,
    "opacity": 0.6
  },
  "encoding": {
    "x": {
      "field": "genetic share",
      "type": "quantitative",
      "title": "Estimated Genetic Share",
      "scale": {"domain": [0, 1]}
    },
    "y": {
      "field": "region",
      "type": "nominal",
      "title": "Ancestry Region",
      "sort": "-x"
    },
    "color": {
      "field": "kit",
      "type": "nominal",
      "title": "Testing Kit",
      "scale": {"scheme": "set2"}
    },
    "row": {
      "field": "twin",
      "type": "nominal",
      "title": "Individual"
    },
    "tooltip": [
      {"field": "kit", "type": "nominal", "title": "Kit"},
      {"field": "region", "type": "nominal", "title": "Region"},
      {"field": "genetic share", "type": "quantitative", "title": "Percentage"}
    ]
  },
  "config": {
    "view": {"stroke": "transparent"},
    "axis": {"grid": true, "gridOpacity": 0.5}
  }
}
'|> as_vegaspec()
```

The graphic above tells the story of uncertainty in consumer DNA
testing. While we might assume that reading DNA is an exact science,
this visualization reveals that different kits interpret the exact same
material (twins) differently. By plotting the estimated percentage on
the X-axis and grouping by ancestry region on the Y-axis, we can clearly
see the "spread" of the colored dots. It proves that these kits are
giving us estimates based on their specific reference panels, not
absolute facts.

## Exercise 2

**Challenge: Identify issues with this graphic and make something
better.** 

![](images/스크린샷 2026-03-19 오전 11.31.36.png){width="426"}

*Issues*

1.  The y-axis runs from 0.00 to 1.25, but the data labels show totals
    of "478,123" and "496,234". The y-axis is likely meant to represent
    units of 100,000 (so 0.50 means 50,000 touchpoints per month), but
    missing the "in 100,000s" label forces the audience to do mental
    math to figure out what the bars represent.

2.  Stacked bars are great for showing totals, but terrible for showing
    individual trends. Because the "Phone" segment at the bottom
    fluctuates, the baselines for "Chat" and "Email" are constantly
    moving up and down. This makes it visually impossible to tell if
    chat or email volumes are actually trending up or down over time.

3.  The horizontal brackets showing the yearly totals (478,123 and
    496,234) have black dots that float arbitrarily and cut right
    through the data bars, creating visual clutter.

*Possible Improvements*

1.  label the y-axis with (in 100K) to show that 0.5 represents 50,000.

2.  Use a Line Chart with three distinct lines—one for Phone, one for
    Chat, and one for Email. This will show individual trend of each
    channel type to resolve the problem of stacked bar.

3.  Exclude the totals (478,123 and 496,234) from the new generated line
    graph, however, if the information is critical or necessary, it is
    always possible to add in the description paragraph afterwards.

**b**

*about the data source* The data used for this graphic is a dataset
containing 7,500 records of user smartphone habits.

dataset: [Where I
downloaded](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/jayjoshi37/smartphone-usage-and-addiction-prediction?resource=download) -
[Raw Dataset
(csv)](https://gist.githubusercontent.com/honggikim02/0d387e86e18464f71f56df29af99b9b8/raw/53a871166ea997c932b3874e6c1a2786a3f0b208/smartphoneaddiction.csv)

**Maximizing the Data-Ink Ratio (Decluttering)**: In accordance with
Tufte’s principles, *non-essential visual clutter* was stripped away. I
removed the default background gridlines to give the data room to
breathe. I also removed redundant legends from the Stress and Age
charts, as the X-axis labels already provided that information clearly.

**Preattentive Attributes (Color)**: In the primary scatterplot, color
is used as a preattentive attribute to immediately separate users by
their "Addicted Status." By using the high-contrast color scheme (red vs
blue), the viewer instantly processes the "wall" where daily screen time
crosses into addiction without having to actively read the axes.

**Data Integrity (Honest Scales)**: A common pitfall in interactive
dashboards is allowing axes to auto-zoom when data is filtered, which
can mislead the viewer about the size of a subset. To maintain visual
integrity, I hardcoded the Y-axis scales. When a viewer highlights a
small cluster of users, the bars shrink relative to the maximum
population, maintaining an honest representation of the total dataset.
Although this might cause difficulties for the viewrs to read the data
at small cluster, I believed it would be a better choice compare to when
the axes scales shift every single time.

**Layering for Context**: Instead of just showing a sleep distribution
histogram, I layered a calculated average rule line (the red vertical
line) with exact text over the bars. This allows the viewer to see both
the shape of the data and the summary statistic simultaneously. Also,
this would help the viewers to know the changes in average even in small
clusters where the bars are very low due to fixed y-axis scale.

**Alternatives** In an earlier iteration, the bottom-right chart simply
showed a single bar for "Average Sleep Hours." I removed this and showed
graphic of a full Histogram Distribution. An average value completely
hides the spread of the data. By showing the distribution, we can
uncover a much more interesting narrative: highly addicted users don't
all get 6 hours of sleep; rather, they are bimodal—some get 4 hours,
while others crash and get 9.

## Exercise 5

1.  **An encoding channel other than x or y**

Where I used it: the color channel extensively.

How it was used: In the scatterplot, I mapped color to the
addicted_label to clearly separate the addicted users (blue) from the
non-addicted users (red). It was also used in the Age chart (using the
teals color scheme) and the Stress chart to give each category a
distinct visual identity.

2.  **Layers**

Where I used it: The "Sleep Distribution & Average" chart in the bottom
right.

How it was used: I used the "layer" to stack three completely different
marks on top of the same X/Y axis. I layered a bar mark (the orange
histogram), a rule mark (the red vertical line), and a text mark (the
exact numerical average) all in one chart space to deliver precise
informations.

3.  **Facets**

\*Note: Although the graphic looks like I used facet to sort multiple
graphs and plots, faceting is used to split a single chart type into
multiple small multiples based on a category. Because I wanted to show
completely different types of charts together, I used concatenation
instead.

4.  **Concatenation or Repeat**

Where I used it: The entire layout of the dashboard.

How it was used: I used "vconcat" (vertical concatenation) to split the
graphic into a top half and a bottom half. Inside those halves, I used
"hconcat" (horizontal concatenation) to place the individual charts
side-by-side.

5.  **Non-default settings for a channel’s scale or guide**

Where I used it: Across almost all the charts (Axes, Domains, and
Colors).

How it was used: - Scale (Domain): As mentioned in Exercise 4, I applied
"scale": {"domain": \[0, 900\]} to the Y-axes of the bar charts. This
non-default setting locks the axis in place so the bars dynamically
shrink when you filter the data, rather than the chart zooming in
confusingly.

-   Scale (Color): I overrode the default color palettes by specifying
    "scale": {"scheme": "set1"} and "scheme": "teals".

-   Guide (Axis): I used "axis": {"labelAngle": 0} to force the text
    labels to sit horizontal instead of tilting diagonally.

6.  **Tooltips**

Where I used it: The scatterplot dots.

How it was used: I fed an array of fields (line 55 - line 59) into the
"tooltip" channel. Now, hovering over a single, anonymous dot reveals a
pop-up with 5 specific data points (Age, Gender, Screen Time, Sleep
Hours, Addicted Status).

7.  **Another kind of interaction (Brushing)**

Where I used it: The main "Screen Time vs. Work/Study Time" scatterplot.

How it was used: I defined a parameter called "brush" configured for
"interval". This allows the user to click and drag a rectangular box
over a cluster of dots. We then applied a "transform": \[{"filter":
{"param": "brush"}}\] to the other three charts, turning the brush into
an interactive, cross-filtering tool that updates the whole dashboard in
real-time.

## Exercise 6

**a. Advanced Vega-Lite Features**

1.  **Global Theming through the `config` Block (Exercise 3 & 4):**
    Rather than manually styling the axes, borders, and fonts for every
    single chart individually, I utilized the top-level `"config"` block
    at the end of my JSON specifications. For example, in the complex
    dashboard for Exercise 4, I used
    `"config": {"view": {"stroke": "transparent"}, "concat": {"spacing": 40}, "axis": {"grid": false}}`.

2.  **Small Multiples through the `row` Encoding Channel (Exercise 1):**
    To show how different testing kits estimated ancestry for the *same*
    individuals, I needed to split the scatterplot. Instead of building
    a complex, nested `"facet"` block, I used the `"row"` encoding
    channel. This is a highly efficient, advanced shortcut in Vega-Lite
    that instantly generates vertically stacked small multiples, giving
    each twin their own dedicated horizontal track.

3.  **Calculated Expressions in Headers (Exercise 1):** In the faceting
    for the twin genetic share graphic, I didn't want the panel headers
    to just show bare numbers or raw data strings. Inside the `"header"`
    block of the facet encoding, I used
    `"labelExpr": "\'Pair \' + datum.value"`. This feature allows you to
    write expressions to dynamically concatenate text and data,
    resulting in much cleaner, reader-friendly labels like "Pair 1"
    instead of just "1".

**b. Application of Graphic Design Principles**

1.  **Titles as Storytelling Tools (Wilke):** Claus O. Wilke emphasizes
    that text is a crucial graphical element and that titles should
    ideally bring the core message or provide instructions, rather than
    just stating the variables. In Exercise 4, instead of a generic
    title like "Scatterplot of Screen Time," I used "The Extremes of
    Smartphone Addiction" alongside an instructional subtitle
    ("Highlight a cluster...").
    -   *Citation:* Wilke, C. O. (2019). *Fundamentals of Data
        Visualization*. O'Reilly Media. Chapter 22: "Titles, captions,
        and tables." (Available at:
        <https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/figure-titles-captions.html>)
2.  **Maximizing the Data-Ink Ratio (Tufte):** Edward Tufte famously
    advocates for erasing non-data-ink to let the actual data stand out.
    Across my portfolio (especially Exercises 3 and 4), I aggressively
    stripped away default programmatic clutter. I explicitly removed the
    chart borders using `"view": {"stroke": "transparent"}` and removed
    the distracting background gridlines (`"axis": {"grid": false}`).
    -   *Citation:* Tufte, E. R. (2001). *The Visual Display of
        Quantitative Information* (2nd ed.). Graphics Press. Chapter 4:
        "Data-Ink and Graphical Redesign."
        [pdf](https://kyl.neocities.org/books/%5BTEC%20TUF%5D%20the%20visual%20display%20of%20quantitative%20information.pdf)
3.  **Avoiding Stacked Bars for Trend Comparisons (Healy):** In Exercise
    2, the original graphic used a stacked bar chart to show changes in
    customer touchpoints over time. Kieran Healy points out that stacked
    bar charts make it extremely difficult to compare the trends of the
    inner or upper segments because they lack a common baseline.
    Following this principle, I redesigned the graphic into a line chart
    with three distinct lines. This allows the viewer to easily and
    accurately track the independent trajectory of Phone, Chat, and
    Email touchpoints.
    -   *Citation:* Healy, K. (2019). *Data Visualization: A practical
        introduction*. Princeton University Press. Chapter 1: "Look at
        data." (Available at: <https://socviz.co/lookatdata.html>)
